summary: Describes Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation, an experimental congestion control scheme for interactive real-time media like video conferencing. The sender adjusts its rate from implicit or explicit congestion signals and can use ECN marks from the network, behaving consistently when marks are absent.

eli5.summary: A video call must not flood the pipe. The sender watches for signs of crowding and slows down or speeds up, a bit like adjusting a faucet.

questions: how does nada handle ecn markings
subtitle: A unified congestion control algorithm for real-time interactive media that reacts to delay, packet loss, and explicit congestion notifications.

tldr.problem: Real-time media applications like video conferencing need congestion control that adapts quickly to bandwidth changes, minimizes queuing delay, and handles variable video encoder output—requirements different from TCP's strict reliability focus.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver continuously measures one-way delay, packet loss, and ECN markings, computing an aggregated congestion signal that accounts for all three. It periodically sends this signal to the sender, which adjusts the sending rate using either accelerated ramp-up (when the network is underutilized) or gradual rate updates (when congestion is detected).
tldr.outcome: Video conferencing and other interactive media get fair bandwidth allocation, adapt quickly to congestion, keep queuing delays low, and work consistently whether the network provides explicit ECN markings or only implicit congestion signals.

today: RFC 8698 is an Experimental specification published in February 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated by later RFCs, and remains the primary specification for NADA congestion control. The experimental status reflects ongoing evaluation in real-world deployments and parameter tuning across different network environments.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Goals
sections.content:
Interactive real-time media applications face congestion control challenges unlike traditional TCP applications. They need to adapt quickly to instantaneous bandwidth changes, accommodate fluctuations in video encoder output rates, and minimize queuing delay to avoid perceptual quality degradation. TCP's mechanisms, designed for bulk data transfer and throughput maximization, do not meet these requirements.

RFC 8698 describes NADA (Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation), an experimental congestion control scheme designed specifically for real-time media. NADA's key innovation is a unified approach: the sender reacts consistently to an aggregated congestion signal that combines multiple indicators—one-way delay (d_queue), packet loss (p_loss), and ECN markings (p_mark)—into a single equivalent delay metric. This unified behavior ensures consistent rate adaptation whether the network provides explicit ECN signals or only implicit loss and delay signals.
sections.eli5: NADA is designed for video calls and live streaming. It watches three traffic lights—delay, lost packets, and explicit network signals—and tells the sender to speed up or slow down based on what it sees.

sections.title: System Overview and Components
sections.content:
NADA operates in a system with four main components. The media encoder produces a compressed bitstream at a target rate r_vin that may fluctuate around its requested rate. The RTP sender calculates a reference rate (r_ref) based on congestion feedback and regulates the actual sending rate (r_send). The RTP receiver measures end-to-end delay, packet loss, ECN marking ratios, and receiving rate (r_recv), then periodically sends an RTCP feedback report containing an aggregated congestion signal (x_curr) and a rate adaptation mode (rmode). Network nodes can operate in multiple modes: simple drop-tail behavior (implicit signals only), RED-based ECN marking, or advanced token-bucket marking.

NADA uses RTP timestamps and standard RTCP feedback; it assumes no per-flow state in network nodes, allowing easy scaling to many video flows. The receiver estimates queuing delay by maintaining the minimum observed one-way delay as a baseline and subtracting it from current measurements, thereby canceling clock offsets between sender and receiver.
sections.eli5: The receiver is like a listener watching the conversation. It measures how long words take to travel, whether packets get lost, and watches for network signals. Every 100 milliseconds it sends back a report saying 'speed up,' 'slow down,' or 'stay steady.'

sections.title: Core Congestion Control Algorithm
sections.content:
The receiver computes an aggregated congestion signal x_curr that combines delay, loss, and marking into a single equivalent delay value. The formula is: x_curr = d_tilde + DMARK*(p_mark/PMRREF)^2 + DLOSS*(p_loss/PLRREF)^2, where d_tilde is optionally warped queuing delay, DMARK is a delay penalty factor for ECN markings at reference ratio PMRREF, and DLOSS is a penalty factor for packet loss at reference ratio PLRREF. When no loss or marking occurs, x_curr reduces to just the queuing delay, enabling pure delay-based adaptation.

The receiver also determines the rate adaptation mode (rmode): accelerated ramp-up when the network appears underutilized (no recent losses, no queuing buildup), or gradual update when congestion is detected. The sender reacts differently to each mode. In ramp-up mode, it increases the reference rate multiplicatively by a factor (gamma) bounded by the round-trip time and maximum queuing delay. In gradual mode, it adjusts the rate using two control terms: an offset term (x_curr minus equilibrium) providing integral control, and a change term (x_diff) providing proportional feedback. The final rate is clipped between RMIN (minimum supported by the media codec) and RMAX (maximum).
sections.eli5: The receiver turns three measurements into one 'congestion number.' When this number is low, the sender ramps up quickly. When it's high and changing, the sender slows down gradually, using math similar to a thermostat.

sections.title: Practical Implementation and Buffer Management
sections.content:
In practical implementation, the receiver maintains a 500 ms observation window (LOGWIN) to estimate packet loss and marking ratios, using exponential smoothing to filter noise. It applies a minimum filter with a 15-sample window to the queuing delay to remove processing spikes. The sender employs a rate-shaping buffer to absorb mismatches between the encoder's actual output rate (r_vout) and the regulated sending rate (r_send). When this buffer builds up, the sender reduces the video encoder target rate (r_vin) and increases the sending rate (r_send) to drain it, bounded by 5% of the reference rate so as not to overwhelm congestion control.

Feedback is sent periodically at a target interval (DELTA = 100 ms recommended) containing the mode (rmode), aggregated congestion signal (x_curr), and receiving rate (r_recv). The algorithm is parameterized with recommended defaults including XREF=10ms (reference congestion level), KAPPA=0.5 and ETA=2.0 (control gains), and TAU=500ms (upper bound on RTT). These parameters can be tuned for specific network conditions and deployment scenarios.
sections.eli5: The sender also manages a buffer like a sink behind a faucet—if water backs up (big buffer), it opens the faucet wider and turns down the tap. Every 100 milliseconds, the receiver sends back a note saying how congested it is.

sections.title: Unified Behavior and Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
NADA's unified behavior means it adapts consistently regardless of which congestion signals the network provides. It can be deployed incrementally: first in networks with only implicit signals (delay and loss), then enhanced as networks adopt ECN marking. This incremental approach facilitates deployment without requiring network-wide coordination. The algorithm guarantees stability for path round-trip times below 250 ms with default parameters and supports weighted bandwidth sharing among multiple flows through the PRIO (priority) parameter, allowing fair coexistence with other NADA flows.

Security considerations include integrity checking of RTCP feedback messages (since the algorithm relies on receiver feedback for rate adaptation). The RFC recommends additional experimentation in real-world settings, especially with ECN-enabled networks, multiple flows with different priorities, and various media types and access technologies (cellular, wireless). Reference implementations are available in ns-2 and ns-3 simulators, and evaluation in Mozilla's WebRTC implementation has validated effectiveness in recovering from throughput drops caused by last-hop wireless congestion.
sections.eli5: NADA works the same way whether the network has modern ECN signals or old-fashioned loss signals. This means it can be deployed anywhere and will gradually work better as networks improve.
